q: Who is the author of the prose lesson "Mijbil the Otter"?
o: Ruskin Bond
Lucio Rodrigues
Gavin Maxwell
Carl Sandburg
e: Gavin Maxwell is the author of "Mijbil the Otter", while Carl Sandburg wrote the poem "Fog".

q: After his dog died, which animal did Gavin Maxwell decide to keep as a pet?
o: An otter
A squirrel
A parrot
A cat
e: Maxwell decided to keep an otter instead of a dog because his home Camusfearna was surrounded by water.

q: What was the name of Gavin Maxwell’s home in Scotland?
o: London Square
Camusfearna
Basra Villa
Dhekiabari
e: Maxwell lived at Camusfearna in the West Highlands of Scotland, ringed by water just a stone’s throw from its door.

q: Where did Gavin Maxwell travel early in the New Year of 1956?
o: Indonesia
Southern Iraq
Egypt
Brazil
e: Early in the New Year of 1956, Gavin Maxwell travelled to Southern Iraq.

q: Where did the author’s friend suggest he could easily get an otter?
o: Amazon rainforest
Sundarbans
Nile delta
Tigris marshes
e: His friend suggested getting an otter in the Tigris marshes, saying they were as common as mosquitoes there.

q: What did the otter look like when he first emerged from the sack? [JAC 2024]
o: A small dragon
A small cat
A small goat
A small dog
e: Coated with symmetrical pointed scales of mud armour, Mijbil resembled a very small dragon.

q: What name did Gavin Maxwell give to his pet otter? [JAC 2023]
o: Jonnie
Mijbil
Custard
Sherry
e: The author named the otter "Mijbil", shortened to "Mij".

q: What scientific name did zoologists give to Mijbil’s previously unknown race of otters?
o: Lutra iraqi maxwelli
Panthera tigris maxwelli
Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli (Maxwell’s otter)
Canis lupus maxwelli
e: Mijbil belonged to a race previously unknown to science and was christened Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli, or Maxwell’s otter.

q: In which city was the Consulate-General where Maxwell received his mail and the otter?
o: Cairo
Tehran
Baghdad
Basra
e: Maxwell and his friend travelled to Basra to collect and answer their mail at the Consulate-General.

q: How long did it take to remove all the mud from Mijbil so that his true colour became visible?
o: One week
One month
One year
One day
e: The mud was caked so deeply that it took a full month before all of it was removed and his true colour showed.

q: What was the colour of Mijbil’s soft velvet fur beneath the mud armour?
o: Snow white
Chocolate-brown like a mole
Golden yellow
Bright blue
e: Between the tips of the mud scales, soft velvet fur like that of a chocolate-brown mole was visible.

q: What size of box did the airline insist Mijbil should be packed in?
o: A thirty-inch glass cage
Larger than forty inches square
Not more than eighteen inches square
A ten-inch round basket
e: The airline insisted that Mijbil be packed into a box not more than eighteen inches square, kept on the floor at Maxwell’s feet.

q: When the British airline refused to fly animals to London, where did Maxwell book a flight to first?
o: Moscow
New Delhi
Rome
Paris
e: Maxwell booked a flight to Paris on another airline, and from there to London.

q: What parcel of food for Mijbil did Maxwell hand over to the air hostess on the flight?
o: A parcel of fish
A bottle of milk
Bread-bangles
A box of cakes
e: Maxwell brought a parcel of fish for Mijbil and entrusted it to the air hostess to keep in a cool place.

q: When Mijbil escaped inside the aircraft, what did a woman stand up and scream?
o: "A lion! A lion!"
"A rat! A rat!"
"A snake! A snake!"
"A thief! A thief!"
e: Confusion broke out in the cabin as a woman stood up on her seat screaming, "A rat! A rat!"

q: In London, with which object did Mijbil invent a game using a ping-pong ball?
o: An empty bucket
A bicycle wheel
Maxwell’s damaged suitcase
A copper pitcher
e: Closing the lid of Maxwell’s damaged suitcase created a slope; Mij placed the ping-pong ball on the high end and raced round to catch it below.

q: Who is the poet of the poem "Fog"? [JAC 2022]
o: Walt Whitman
W.B. Yeats
Robert Frost
Carl Sandburg
e: American poet Carl Sandburg wrote the six-line poem "Fog".

q: In the poem "Fog", what animal’s feet does the fog come on?
o: Little cat feet
Horse hooves
Swift deer hooves
Big dog paws
e: The poem opens with: "The fog comes / on little cat feet."

q: In the poem "Fog", what does the fog sit looking over?
o: Forests and mountains
Harbour and city
Deserts and villages
Rivers and farms
e: The poem states that the fog sits looking "over harbour and city".

q: In what posture does the fog sit in Carl Sandburg’s poem?
o: Spreading wide wings
On silent haunches
Hanging from a branch
Galloping furiously
e: Like a seated cat, the fog rests "on silent haunches" before moving on.

q: How does the poem "Fog" conclude regarding the departure of the fog?
o: "And sinks into the earth"
"And fights the sun"
"And then roars in thunder"
"And then moves on"
e: The final line "and then moves on" captures the quiet, unannounced departure of the fog.

q: Which small toys did Mijbil especially love juggling on his wide, flat belly without dropping them?
o: Marbles
Playing cards
Iron nails
Glass bangles
e: Mijbil loved lying on his back and rolling two or more marbles up and down his wide, flat belly without ever dropping one.

q: What building stood opposite Gavin Maxwell’s London flat, with a low wall Mijbil loved to gallop along?
o: A railway station
A primary school
A large hospital
A city zoo
e: Opposite his flat was a primary school fronted by a low wall about two feet high and thirty yards long.

q: After how many days of waiting and cabling England did Maxwell’s mail finally arrive in Basra?
o: One month
Two days
Five days
Ten days
e: After telephone failures and holidays delayed two cables, Maxwell’s mail finally arrived after five days.

q: Who brought the squirming sack containing the otter into Maxwell’s bedroom in Basra?
o: Post-office clerks
Two British diplomats
Two police officers
Two Arabs
e: Two Arabs squatted on the bedroom floor beside a squirming sack and handed him a note from his friend.

q: How did Mijbil behave during his first twenty-four hours with Gavin Maxwell?
o: Neither hostile nor friendly, simply aloof and indifferent
Immediately climbing onto his lap
Barking continuously
Fiercely aggressive
e: For the first twenty-four hours Mijbil was neither hostile nor friendly; he stayed aloof and indifferent, sleeping on the floor.

q: What did Mijbil do when Maxwell first took him into the bathroom?
o: Fled in terror of water
Went wild with joy in the water for half an hour, plunging and rolling
Fell asleep beside the drain
Shredded the bath towel
e: On reaching the bathtub, Mijbil went wild with joy for half an hour, plunging, rolling, and splashing water everywhere.

q: Two days later in the bathroom, what astonishing feat did Mijbil perform with his paws?
o: Wiped the bathroom mirror
Locked the latch from inside
Turned on the chromium tap himself to produce a full flow of water
Washed a towel with soap
e: Standing on the bathtub, Mijbil fumbled with the chromium tap and within a minute turned it on to full flow.

q: How far was the airport when Maxwell rushed out with just ten minutes remaining before the flight?
o: Twenty miles
Fifty miles
One mile
Five miles
e: With only ten minutes left until flight time, the airport was five miles distant.

q: What surprising question did a street labourer digging a hole in London growl at Maxwell?
o: "Here, Mister — what is that supposed to be?"
"Will you sell this creature to me?"
"How many pounds does it cost?"
"Does this monkey drink tea?"
e: Laying down his tools and glaring, the labourer growled: "Here, Mister — what is that supposed to be?"

q: What was written on the note from Maxwell’s friend delivered with the sack?
o: "Beware, this creature bites."
"Here is your otter..."
"Return this immediately."
"This is a rare river fish."
e: The note from his friend simply read: "Here is your otter..."

q: How did Mijbil’s behaviour change on the second night with Maxwell?
o: He refused food for three days
He jumped out of the window
He came onto the bed in the small hours and slept in the crook of Maxwell’s knees till morning tea
He tore up all the curtains
e: On the second night Mijbil climbed onto the bed in the small hours and remained asleep in the crook of Maxwell’s knees until tea arrived.

q: According to Maxwell, what is the unmistakable characteristic of otters regarding water?
o: Water should never touch their fur
Water is meant only for drinking quietly
Water should remain frozen still
Water must be kept on the move and made to splash; static water is wasted and provoking
e: Maxwell explains that otters believe every drop of water must be kept on the move and made to splash; static water provokes them.

q: How did Mijbil react on the occasion when he accidentally turned the bathroom tap the wrong way?
o: He chittered with irritation and disappointment at the tap’s failure to cooperate
He bit Maxwell’s hand
He barked loudly at the mirror
He calmly walked back to bed
e: When he turned the tap the wrong way and got no trickle, he chittered with irritation and disappointment at its refusal to cooperate.

q: How did Mijbil move a rubber ball around the room?
o: Like a cricket batsman
Like a four-footed soccer player dribbling the ball
Like a golf player
Like a badminton champion
e: He spent hours shuffling a rubber ball round the room like a four-footed soccer player using all four feet to dribble it.

q: What appalling spectacle greeted Maxwell when he returned after leaving Mijbil in the box for an hour?
o: The wooden box had vanished
Mijbil was peacefully sleeping inside
Complete silence hung over the box while blood had trickled and dried around the airholes
Mijbil had eaten his snack peacefully
e: Mijbil had torn the sharp lining to shreds trying to escape, leaving him exhausted and blood-spattered with dried blood around the chinks.

q: What did Maxwell spread over the floor around his feet inside the aircraft?
o: Soft feather cushions
Banana leaves
A silk carpet
Parcels of newspapers
e: Maxwell covered the floor around his feet with parcels of newspapers before settling in.

q: Why did Maxwell describe the air hostess as "the very queen of her kind"?
o: Because she listened kindly to his crisis, took the fish, and even suggested keeping Mij on his knee
Because she gave him a free ticket
Because she came from Camusfearna
Because she belonged to royal nobility
e: She listened compassionately to the distressing events, stored the fish, and kindly advised keeping Mij on his knee.

q: When Maxwell dived to grab Mijbil’s tail in the aeroplane aisle, what ended up covering his face?
o: Hot coffee
Curry
Tomato soup
Orange juice
e: Diving for Mij’s tail and missing, Maxwell found his face covered in curry.

q: How did Mijbil finally return to Maxwell on the aeroplane?
o: He jumped out of the hatch
The pilot tied him up inside the cockpit
He bounded onto Maxwell’s knee with a chitter of recognition and nuzzled his face and neck
He fell asleep inside a suitcase
e: Soon Mij appeared from down the aisle, bounded onto Maxwell’s knee with a chitter of recognition, and nuzzled his face and neck.

q: About how long did Maxwell stay with Mijbil in his London flat?
o: Two full years
Six months
Only three days
Nearly a month
e: Maxwell writes that Mij and he remained in London for nearly a month.

q: Which compulsive habit did Mijbil develop during walks in London?
o: Tugging Maxwell to the primary school’s low outer wall and galloping its full thirty-yard length
Entering every bakery
Snatching hats from passersby
Biting car tyres
e: Like children stepping on paving squares, Mij always jumped onto the primary school’s two-foot wall and galloped all thirty yards, distracting pupils and staff.

q: Which of these wild guesses did Londoners make about what kind of animal Mijbil was?
o: Baby elephant, giraffe, and kangaroo
Baby seal, squirrel, walrus, hippo, beaver, bear cub, leopard, and brontosaur
White tiger and giant panda
Penguin and dolphin
e: Londoners guessed Mij was a baby seal, squirrel, walrus, hippo, beaver, bear cub, a spot-changed leopard, and even a brontosaur.

q: What happened inside the primary school whenever Mijbil galloped along its thirty-yard outer wall?
o: Teachers brought him inside to lecture
All pupils studied more quietly
It caused hopeless distraction to both pupils and staff
The school closed permanently
e: Maxwell writes that Mij’s gallop along the thirty-yard wall happened "to the hopeless distraction both of pupils and of staff."

q: Which phrase did Maxwell use to describe the new phase of his life that began with Mijbil?
o: Passing boredom
Unbearable burden
Business partnership
"Thralldom to otters" (an otter fixation)
e: Maxwell calls it the second phase of his life—"a thralldom to otters, an otter fixation" that he shared with other otter owners.

q: Why was Gavin Maxwell reluctant to keep another dog after Jonnie died?
o: Dogs were banned in Scotland
Dogs refused to travel to Iraq
He lacked outdoor space
He was too heartbroken over his pet dog Jonnie’s death to consider keeping another dog
e: Grief over losing his beloved dog Jonnie made Maxwell unwilling to replace him with another dog, leading him to consider an otter.

q: What does Mijbil’s suitcase-and-ping-pong-ball game reveal about his intelligence?
o: He only copied dogs blindly
He possessed sharp curiosity and inventiveness to create self-amusing games using gravity
He disliked round toys
He preferred sleeping all afternoon
e: Placing the ball on the high slope and racing to intercept it before it rolled off shows remarkable inventiveness and spatial awareness.

q: What flaw in the wooden box injured Mijbil before the flight?
o: The box was too huge
The box flooded with rainwater
Mijbil tore the inner lining to shreds and cut himself on its sharp jagged edges
There were no airholes at all
e: Mijbil had ripped the lining inside to shreds, injuring himself against the jagged, sharp surfaces left exposed.

q: How did the driver drive Maxwell’s car to the airport in the final ten minutes?
o: Stopping twice for fuel
At walking speed
At a snail’s pace
Like a ricochetting bullet
e: With barely ten minutes left, Maxwell sat in the back while the driver tore through the streets "like a ricochetting bullet."

q: How many lines are there in Carl Sandburg’s poem "Fog"?
o: Six lines
Ten lines
Fourteen lines
Four lines
e: "Fog" is a compact six-line free-verse poem.

q: What poetic style does the brevity and nature imagery of "Fog" most closely resemble?
o: Heroic epic
Haiku-like / Imagist nature miniature
Mourning elegy
Shakespearean sonnet
e: Its crisp brevity, unrhymed lines, and vivid single nature image echo the Imagist / Haiku-like miniature tradition.

q: Which three actions in "Fog" mirror both a cat and the fog?
o: Swimming, flying, and hiding
Running, roaring, and sleeping
Coming silently, sitting watchfully on haunches, and moving on quietly
Pouncing, mewing, and scratching
e: Just like a cat, fog arrives quietly ("little cat feet"), sits watchfully ("silent haunches"), and slips away ("moves on").

q: What obstacles delayed Maxwell’s telegrams and mail in Basra?
o: A fire at the post office
A sunken ship
War and floods
A breakdown on the line, an exchange closed for a religious holiday, and another day’s break
e: On the first day the line had broken down, the next the exchange closed for a religious holiday, and on the third another breakdown occurred.

q: Why did Londoners fail to recognise Mijbil as an otter?
o: Because otters are not among the animals commonly recognised in London
Because he walked only at midnight
Because he changed colour like a chameleon
Because Mijbil wore a winter coat
e: Maxwell observes it is not surprising Londoners failed, as otters are rarely seen in the city and people made wild guesses.

q: How did Mijbil respond when called by his shortened name "Mij"?
o: He hid under the sofa
He followed Maxwell without a lead and came when called by name
He plugged his ears
He ignored it completely
e: Soon Mijbil lost his apathy, took keen interest in his surroundings, and followed Maxwell when called by name.

q: How did Maxwell manage to board the aircraft despite arriving at the last minute?
o: He waited till the next day
He hired a private plane
The aircraft was waiting to take off as he rushed through angry officials
The pilot was his cousin
e: The plane was actually waiting to take off; Maxwell sprinted past infuriated airport officials directly to his seat.

q: In Carl Sandburg’s poem "Fog", what does the word "harbour" refer to?
o: A flower garden
A desert dune
A mountain peak
A sheltered port or coastal waters where ships dock
e: "Harbour" means a port where ships shelter; coastal fog famously rolls in silently from the harbour across the city.

q: During walks in London, which habit of Mijbil resembled the superstitions of human children?
o: Developing compulsive habits like placing paws squarely on every paving block or walking inside specific railings
Saluting every dog
Singing at traffic signals
Dancing under every lamp post
e: Maxwell compared Mij’s habits—like lunging onto the exact same wall every walk—to children’s rituals with paving blocks and iron railings.

q: What atmosphere does Carl Sandburg create in "Fog" by using the cat metaphor?
o: Violent earthquake and panic
Quiet mystery, stealth, watchful stillness, and fleeting presence
Roaring thunder and hail
Scorching summer heatwave
e: The cat metaphor evokes hushed stillness, stealthy observation, and the quiet unpredictability of nature.

q: By the end of "Mijbil the Otter", how did Maxwell’s experiment of keeping an otter instead of a dog turn out?
o: Pointless and boring
A complete failure as Mij escaped
Deeply rewarding and affectionate, binding Maxwell into lifelong fascination with otters
Declared illegal by the court
e: Through Mijbil’s intelligence, playfulness, and deep affection, the experiment succeeded wonderfully and fostered a lifelong devotion.

q: In "ringed by water a stone’s throw from its door", what does the idiom "a stone’s throw" mean?
o: Across the ocean
A dangerous rocky zone
Many miles away
At a very short distance
e: "A stone’s throw" is an idiom meaning a very short distance away.

q: In "he was simply aloof and indifferent", what does "aloof" mean?
o: Distant, reserved, and emotionally detached
Extremely cunning
Deeply terrified
Fiercely quarrelsome
e: "Aloof" means coolly distant or detached—Mij kept to himself on the first night in an unfamiliar room.

q: When Maxwell says static water is "provoking" to an otter, what does "provoking" mean here?
o: Soothing and peaceful
Irritating or arousing an urge to overturn/splash it
Sweet-tasting
Suitable for drinking quietly
e: Static water annoys and challenges an otter’s playful instinct, urging him to overturn or splash it until it moves.

q: In "I saw an appalling spectacle", what does "appalling" convey about what Maxwell saw?
o: Ordinary and dull
Charming and delightful
Horrifying and deeply shocking
Hilariously funny
e: "Appalling" means causing dismay or horror—Maxwell was horrified to see dried blood and an exhausted Mijbil.

q: In "there began a thralldom to otters", what does "thralldom" mean?
o: Financial debt
Legal ownership
Hatred and fear
The state of being captivated or completely fascinated
e: "Thralldom" means being held under an irresistible spell or deep fascination—exactly what Maxwell felt toward otters.

q: Which primary poetic device is used in "The fog comes / on little cat feet"?
o: Metaphor
Pun
Hyperbole
Simile
e: Sandburg compares fog directly to a cat without using "like" or "as", creating a sustained Metaphor.

q: In "It sits looking / over harbour and city", besides metaphor, which literary device gives fog the deliberate act of sitting and watching?
o: Personification
Oxymoron
Anastrophe
Alliteration
e: Giving natural weather the intentional action of "sitting and looking" acts as Personification (within the extended cat metaphor).

q: What kind of imagery is created by "It sits looking ... on silent haunches" in "Fog"?
o: Rough tactile imagery
Visual and quietness/stillness imagery
Sharp olfactory imagery
Sweet gustatory imagery
e: It evokes vivid visual imagery of a poised cat resting silently, mirroring fog blanketing the harbour and city without a sound.

q: Why did Carl Sandburg avoid saying "like a cat" in "Fog", using an extended metaphor instead of a simile?
o: Because cats never walk near harbours
To lengthen the poem to twenty lines
A metaphor fuses fog and cat into a single living image, making the six-line poem far tighter and more evocative
He disliked the word "like"
e: Extended metaphor merges fog and cat seamlessly without explicit comparison words, giving the miniature poem maximum punch.

q: What does Mijbil responding to "Mij" and following Maxwell without a leash in Basra indicate?
o: High intelligence and rapid emotional bonding between an otter and an attentive human
Mij was unable to walk straight
Maxwell starved him into obedience
Otters are sluggish creatures
e: Moving from Day 1 aloofness to following his name shows an otter’s remarkable intelligence and capacity to bond.

q: What quality of Mijbil is demonstrated when he fumbles with the chromium tap until he gets a full flow of water?
o: Curiosity, observational learning, and problem-solving ability
Fear of flowing water
Poor eyesight
Sheer laziness
e: Observing how taps work and manipulating the lever until water flows proves keen observational learning and problem-solving skill.

q: How did the air hostess handle the chaos after Mijbil escaped inside the aircraft?
o: She threatened to arrest Maxwell
She demanded an emergency landing
She reassured Maxwell calmly to return to his seat and helped locate the otter gently
She jumped onto a seat screaming too
e: Showing calm professionalism and kindness, she reassured Maxwell to sit back down while she looked after locating the otter.

q: Why did London passersby compare Mijbil to a beaver, baby seal, or bear cub rather than an otter?
o: Because otters look identical to polar bears
Because books were banned in London
Because city residents had never seen a live otter and matched his unfamiliar traits to creatures they knew
Because Mij changed shape every hour
e: People naturally classify unfamiliar sights using familiar references—since otters were unseen in London, they guessed similar-looking animals.

q: When Maxwell found Mijbil injured inside the metal-lined box, why was the moment especially heartbreaking for him?
o: Because his expensive suit was stained
Because the airline refused a refund
Because his meal had gone cold
Because he had unintentionally put Mij in danger and still had to put the terrified, wounded creature back to catch the flight in ten minutes
e: He had inadvertently exposed Mij to sharp edges and, with just ten minutes to catch the flight, still had to place the shaken animal back inside.

q: How does the short, broken lineation of "Fog" support the meaning of the poem?
o: A loud military marching beat
The slow, unhurried, quiet pacing of a cat arriving, pausing, and slipping away
The clatter of a rushing train
The crash of thunderstorm waves
e: Short enjambed phrases mimic the measured, noiseless pacing of a cat stepping softly, pausing, and gliding away.

q: The Londoner’s remark "a leopard, one that had changed its spots" plays on which English proverb?
o: "Slow and steady wins the race"
The proverb "A leopard cannot change its spots"
"Look before you leap"
"All that glitters is not gold"
e: It humorously inverts the proverb "A leopard cannot change its spots" to mock how wildly baffled Londoners were.

q: Why did Maxwell’s friend say otters in the Tigris marshes were "as common as mosquitoes"?
o: Because otters are tiny insects
Because otters bite every visitor
Because otters fly in swarms
As humorous exaggeration (hyperbole) stressing their sheer abundance in the Tigris marshes
e: It is humorous hyperbole emphasising how plentiful otters were in the Tigris marshes and how easy it was to obtain one there.

q: Why did Maxwell award "highest marks" to the street labourer’s question "Here, Mister — what is that supposed to be?"?
o: Because instead of making an absurd guess, he bluntly and comically voiced utter bewilderment
Because he offered to buy the otter
Because he was Maxwell’s neighbour
Because the labourer spoke poor English
e: Unlike others making ridiculous guesses, the labourer’s blunt, comical honesty captured everyone’s utter bewilderment.

q: What remarkable juggling skill did Mijbil perform specifically with marbles?
o: He swallowed them whole
Lying on his back, he rolled two or more up and down his wide, flat belly without ever dropping one
He smashed them against windowpanes
He buried them under carpets
e: His balance and paw coordination were so exact that he could roll two or more marbles across his flat belly without dropping any.

q: In "Fog", what quality of nature is underscored by the concluding phrase "and then moves on"?
o: Unchanging urban traffic
Nature’s fleeting, transient, and unpredictable rhythm—fog lingers briefly and departs silently
Permanent winter weather
Human immortality
e: Just like a restless cat, fog cannot be possessed or predicted; it visits briefly and silently continues on its way.

q: How does Mijbil’s transformation from a mud-armoured "small dragon" to sleek chocolate-brown velvet velvet mirror the author’s bond with him?
o: The otter falling sick from soap
A desert dust storm
Care, patience, and familiarity gradually reveal hidden warmth and beauty beneath a strange, guarded exterior
Sudden tropical storms in Basra
e: Patient care washed away both the literal mud and initial aloofness, revealing beauty, trust, and affectionate companionship.

q: How does keeping Mijbil in a London flat differ from Maxwell’s original vision for him at Camusfearna?
o: Every London flat has a wild river inside
Camusfearna is an arid desert
In London Mij stayed inside an iron cage
Camusfearna offered natural open water at the doorstep, whereas in London Mij had to adapt using bathtubs, toys, and leashed walks
e: Despite shifting from Scottish waters to an urban flat, Mij’s remarkable adaptability let him invent games indoors and outdoors.

q: In the aeroplane scene, what do Maxwell’s honesty about the box mishap and the air hostess’s reaction show?
o: Honest communication paired with genuine human empathy turns potential crises into manageable, kind moments
Passengers should hide rules from crew
Airline staff care only for tickets
Pets can never survive flights
e: Maxwell’s candid honesty met with genuine empathy from the air hostess resolved a stressful predicament gracefully.

q: Why did the ping-pong ball keep rolling down Maxwell’s damaged suitcase during Mijbil’s favourite London game?
o: Because Maxwell kept shaking the suitcase
Because a magnet sat inside the suitcase
Because damage caused the closed lid to remain slanted from one end to the other, creating a ramp
Because the London flat floor was tilted
e: The damaged lid stayed at a natural slant when closed, turning the suitcase into an accidental inclined ramp for the ball.

q: In Carl Sandburg’s "Fog", what does the word "haunches" mean?
o: Fish gills
Tree roots
Bird wings
The back legs and hips on which an animal sits
e: "Haunches" refers to the hindquarters/hips of an animal sitting alertly with front paws ready to move at any moment.

q: Based on the flight preparation in "Mijbil the Otter", what food did Maxwell carry for Mijbil?
o: Fish
Apples and bananas
Only warm milk
Boiled rice
e: Being an aquatic carnivore, Mijbil ate fish, which is why Maxwell brought a parcel of fish for the flight.

q: When Mijbil once escaped into the bathroom on his own before Maxwell entered, what was Mijbil doing?
o: Staring at his reflection in the mirror
Standing up on end on the bathtub, fumbling at the chromium taps with his paws
Eating toilet paper rolls
Shaping soap bars into balls
e: Maxwell watched in amazement as Mij stood on the bathtub edge turning the chromium tap with his paws until water gushed out.

q: How many complete sentences make up the entire six-line poem "Fog"?
o: Six sentences
One sentence
Two sentences
Four sentences
e: There are only two sentences in the whole poem: one describing its silent arrival, and one describing it sitting and moving on.

q: What tone does Gavin Maxwell maintain even while recounting chaotic events like the flight and London walks?
o: Dry technical textbook jargon
Bleak despair
Harsh anger and bitterness
Gentle humour, affectionate warmth, and vivid observational storytelling
e: From curry splashing on his face to Londoners calling Mij a brontosaur, Maxwell’s gentle humour and affection enliven every episode.

q: What major structural feature do Carl Sandburg’s "Fog" and Adrienne Rich’s "The Trees" share?
o: Both follow an AABB rhyme scheme
Both are fourteen-line sonnets
Both feature fire-breathing dragons
Both are composed in free verse without regular rhyme scheme and rely on vivid nature imagery
e: Both "Fog" and "The Trees" use free verse and evocative natural imagery rather than traditional rhyming patterns.

q:
Assertion (A): Gavin Maxwell decided to keep an otter as a pet instead of a dog.
Reason (R): His Scottish home Camusfearna was ringed by water just a stone’s throw from its door, making it eminently suitable.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
